name: Hidden Complexity in Loops
intent: Spot the loop that looks like one pass over n items but quietly does another pass, copy or query inside it, so the cost is n times n and not n, and know the standard fix for each.
scenario: A nightly export reads n order ids, drops duplicates, joins each with a customer row, builds one big string and drains a work list from the front. Every line reads like a single loop and the code passes review. At 1,000 ids it takes milliseconds. At 50,000 the deduplication alone is over a billion steps, and the whole job is the thing that wakes someone up.
problem: Big O is easy to read off a loop you can see and hard to read off a call you cannot. `if x in items`, `list.remove(0)`, `s += piece` and `orders.customer` each look like one operation and each can hide a scan, a shift, a copy or a database round trip that grows with n. Put one inside a loop over n and the cost is quadratic, with no nested loop anywhere in your code. It stays invisible while data is small, so tests pass and the problem arrives with production data.

howItWorks.title: Find the loop you cannot see
howItWorks.text: For every call inside a loop body ask what it costs as a function of n, not just whether it is a function call. Searching a plain list (`x in list`, `list.contains`, `indexOf`) scans it. Removing or inserting at the front of an array or list typically shifts every later element. Counting with a method that walks the structure, or sorting inside the loop, costs a pass or more each time. A regex or substring search over a big text is a scan. The loop's cost is the iteration count times the cost of its most expensive call.

howItWorks.title: Recognise the usual suspects
howItWorks.text: Four patterns cover most cases. Membership test against a list inside a loop: O(n) per test, O(n²) in total. Front removal from an array: O(n) per removal. String building with `s = s + piece`: in many languages and typically, each step copies the whole string so far, though some runtimes optimise particular cases, so do not rely on it. Lookup per row, by scanning another collection for the matching row. A fifth is not in your process at all: lazy loading in an ORM issues one query per row, the N+1 pattern.

howItWorks.title: Build the index once
howItWorks.text: Most fixes replace the repeated scan with a structure built once. Put the ids in a set or dictionary (average cost per lookup is constant), then the loop does n lookups instead of n scans. The price is memory for the structure and a one-off build of n steps, which pays for itself as soon as there is more than a handful of lookups.

howItWorks.title: Use the structure made for the access pattern
howItWorks.text: If you take from the front, use a queue or deque, or move an index instead of deleting. If you append many pieces to a string, collect them in a list or builder and join once, so each character is copied about once. If rows need related rows, fetch them in one batched query or a join and index the result, or use a batching layer such as a DataLoader, instead of one query per row.

howItWorks.title: Hoist what does not change, then measure
howItWorks.text: A value that is the same on every iteration (a length, a count, a compiled regex, a sorted copy, a config lookup) is computed once before the loop. Then confirm with a profile or an operation count on realistic data: runtimes differ, some fast paths exist, and the constant factors matter at small n. The aim is not to ban `in list`, which is fine on 20 items, but to know where n can grow.

pros: Turns a quadratic job into a linear one with a small, local change, often a single line
The fixed structures (set, dictionary, queue, builder) are in the standard library of most languages
Makes the real cost visible in review: every call in a loop gets a question about its cost
The N+1 fix also removes network round trips, which usually dominate the cost
cons: The fixed version uses more memory (a set or dictionary of n entries) and costs a build step
On small inputs the naive version can be as fast or faster, and simpler to read, so the fix can be wasted effort
Hash-based fixes depend on a good hash function and hashable, stable keys
Runtime optimisations make some naive code fast in one language and version and slow in another, so the problem is hard to reproduce
whenToUse: Any loop over data that grows with users, rows, events or files
Code reviews of loops that call a lookup, remove, insert, sort or query in the body
After a slowdown that appeared only with production-sized data
whenNotToUse: Collections that are small and bounded for good (a list of 10 settings): the plain list is clearer
Before you know it is hot: profile first and fix the loops that matter
Fixes that add a hidden cost of their own, such as a cache or index that is rebuilt on every call
pitfalls: Reading `if x in items` as a single step: on a list it scans, on a set or dictionary it is a hash lookup on average
Removing from the front of an array in a loop (`pop(0)`, `shift`, `remove(0)`, `RemoveAt(0)`): each removal typically shifts the rest, so draining n items costs about n²/2 moves
Trusting that string concatenation in a loop is always fine: some runtimes optimise it, many do not, and the code looks identical either way. Joining once is safe everywhere

Assuming `len`, `count` or `size` is O(1): it is for arrays and most built-in collections, but on a hand-written linked list, a lazily evaluated sequence or a database it can mean a full walk or a query
Sorting, or building a regex, inside the loop when the input does not change between iterations
ORM lazy loading: reading `order.customer` for each order issues one query per order (N+1). The loop is O(n) in your code and n queries over the network. See GraphQL N+1 and DataLoader
Fixing the loop but not the data structure around it, for example a set rebuilt from the list on every iteration, which is the same quadratic cost
Optimising every loop on the way, instead of the ones where n can grow, and so making simple code harder to read for no gain

quiz.question: A loop goes over 10,000 rows and for each one checks `if row.key in allowed`, where `allowed` is a list of 10,000 keys. About how many comparisons can that take?
options: About 10,000, since the loop makes one pass over the rows.
Up to about 100 million, since every membership test scans the list.
About 14, because membership tests halve the list each time.
About 20,000, once for each of the two collections.
quiz.explanation: The loop runs 10,000 times and each `in` on a list can scan up to 10,000 entries, so the worst case is about 10,000 x 10,000 = 100 million. A set makes each test a hash lookup on average, which brings the total down to about 10,000.

quiz.question: A function builds a report by doing `text = text + line` for 100,000 lines. Which statement is the safest to rely on?
options: It is always linear, because strings are copied lazily.
It is always quadratic, because every runtime copies the whole string.
It is linear in Python and quadratic everywhere else.
It may be optimised in some runtimes, but collecting lines and joining once is linear everywhere.
quiz.explanation: Whether repeated concatenation copies the growing string depends on the language, version and even the code around it. Collecting the pieces and joining once copies each character about once, whatever the runtime does, so it is the version you do not have to reason about.

quiz.question: A page loads 200 orders, then reads each order's customer lazily, one query per order. Each query costs 2 ms of round trip. How much time goes to those queries?
options: About 402 ms for 201 queries, against about 4 ms with one batched query.
About 2 ms, because the queries run at the same time.
About 200 ms, because the first query for the orders is free.
About 4 ms, because the database caches the customer table.
quiz.explanation: 1 query for the orders plus 200 for their customers is 201 round trips, about 402 ms. Fetching the customers in one batched query takes 2 round trips in total, about 4 ms (a single join that returns orders with their customers takes 1). The extra cost is network round trips, not CPU.
